schools.summary: Gill accounts for the disproportionate herds by a stronger bent to the pastoral life; Calvin traces it to the Egyptian district they had lived in, and reads the seeing of the land as self-interest blinding men to an obligation laid on them by God.

Henry sets the request in the pause in the plains of Moab, notes it was granted at the tribes' request rather than by divine appointment, and names the lust of the eye and the pride of life as its two springs.
Keil and Delitzsch locate Jazer and Gilead and explain the apposition that emphasises the multitude; Ellicott adds that Reuben and Gad had encamped together for thirty-eight years.
Wesley identifies Jazer as an Amorite city and country and Gilead as mountainous pasture land.

Gill follows Aben Ezra in making the Gadites the authors of the scheme, which explains why they are named first; Calvin praises the modesty of a petition sought by permission rather than seized, while faulting the private interest behind it.
Henry reads the inverted order the same way and adds Jacob's sentence on Reuben, that he should not excel.
Keil and Delitzsch take the clause about the land the LORD smote as marking territory now without a ruler, and read "let us not go over the Jordan" in the milder sense.
Gill identifies the towns as Amorite, taken from Sihon, and places Jazer some fifteen miles from Heshbon.
Clarke assigns the places to the kingdoms of Sihon and Og, which became Israelite territory by conquest.
Keil and Delitzsch treat the roll of names as the definition of the country asked for and defer the geography to the closing section.

fidelity.note: the second paragraph is the summary's own framing of why the geography is deferred; the deferral is Keil and Delitzsch's, and the later redistribution of the towns is Ellicott's at v.34, but the contrast between claim and inventory is not drawn by any witness

schools.summary: Gill ascribes the conquest to the LORD and infers that Moses, Eleazar and the princes, as representatives of the people, had the right to dispose of the land.
Keil and Delitzsch read the clause as a legal description of land without a ruler, and note the construction of the verb of giving.
Henry allows that on its own terms the motion was not unreasonable, the land belonging to Israel in common and this being about their supposed proportion.

fidelity.note: the closing paragraph frames the request as a syllogism whose flaw lies in the conclusion; the criticism is Calvin's and Henry's, but the syllogism itself is the summary's own construction

schools.summary: Ellicott gives the two possible senses of "bring us not over Jordan", prefers the stronger, and notes that these tribes were among the first carried into Assyrian captivity.
Gill notes the modest and respectful manner in which the request was addressed to Moses.
Clarke gives the plain motive, that the land was good for pasturage and they had many flocks.
Henry lists what the petition looked like at first sight — contempt of the promise, distrust of God's power, covetousness, neglect of the brethren — and the precedent it would have set.

debates.question: What does "bring us not over Jordan" actually ask for?

sides.position: only that their inheritance be assigned east of the river, without withdrawing help from the conquest
that the conquest of the west be left to the other tribes, so that they may settle at once in land already subdued

schools.summary: Gill records that Moses was displeased, the motion having the appearance of covetousness and cowardice; Calvin insists the vehemence was neither warmth nor error, since the request would lacerate the body of the Church, and holds their ingratitude to God the heavier count.
Henry imputes the heat to pious zeal against sin rather than the peevishness of age, and generalises the rebuke to all who sit unconcerned in their brethren's perils.
Wesley catches the contrast the question is built on: ease and peace here, a bloody war there.

Gill counts the military loss but thinks the moral discouragement worse, the request carrying a distrust of ever possessing Canaan; Calvin had already located the danger in hearts broken so that they refuse the call of God.

Ellicott renders the verb as to alienate or avert and notes its cognate in the account of the spies; Keil and Delitzsch give the idiom as holding the heart away, and set the charge in its sequence toward the wrath of God.
Henry supplies the reckoning a general would make, two tribes and a half being above a fifth part of Israel's strength.

themes: the fifth part of the strength

schools.summary: Gill takes "your fathers" of the whole generation, not the two tribes only; Calvin makes the imitation of ungodly parents double rather than excuse the guilt, compares Stephen and the psalm of provocation, and narrows the comparison to the ten spies from whom the sedition arose.

9.pericope_label: Moses recites the report from Eshcol and the oath that followed

schools.summary: Gill supplies the geography of Eshcol and the cluster it was named from, and marks the double object of the anger — the spies and the people who murmured; Calvin fastens on the ground of the oath, that nothing is praiseworthy unless men persevere to the goal.
Gill weighs whether Caleb or Jephunneh is the Kenezite, prefers Jephunneh, derives the name from an ancestor called Kenaz, and reports Jarchi's contrary account.
Clarke holds flatly that Jephunneh was the Kenezite and Kenaz probably his father; Wesley takes Kenaz to be the grandfather.
Ellicott passes over the genealogy and points to the commendation quoted from the earlier sentence, that they wholly followed the LORD.

debates.question: Who is called "the Kenezite", and from whom is the name taken?

sides.position: Jephunneh, not Caleb, and the name from an ancestor called Kenaz
Jephunneh, whose father was probably Kenaz himself
Caleb was son-in-law to Kenaz, and his mother bore Othniel to him

schools.summary: Gill attaches the kindled anger to the murmuring that followed the spies' report.
Ellicott identifies the forty years as the fulfilment of the prediction Moses himself announced by divine commandment when the evil report was brought up.

fidelity.note: Ellicott supplies the identification of the forty years as the fulfilment Moses himself announced; the second paragraph draws out what that means for the men listening, which is the summary's framing rather than his comment

schools.summary: Gill takes the succession to cover families, substance and manners alike; Calvin reads the noun as a climax — literally an increase, hence a heap — and makes the new generation fuel added to a smouldering fire.
Henry sets the increase of men against the increase of sinful men, and grieves that a rising generation should be worse than the one before it.

themes: risen up in your fathers' stead

schools.summary: Gill glosses turning away as ceasing to follow God in his word, worship and ordinances, and to walk after the pillar of cloud and fire.
Keil and Delitzsch render the idiom as drawing back behind him, and take the two clauses as a longer desert and a destruction the petitioners themselves would prepare.
Henry warns of wrath brought on the whole congregation and draws the maxim that men who considered the end of sin would fear its beginnings.
Henry reconstructs the consultation behind the reply and weighs both possibilities — an honest intention misinterpreted, or plain dealing bringing them to their duty.

Gill notes the freedom and boldness of men who came nearer to speak again; Calvin credits the severity of the rebuke with the change, and reckons the middle course they devise leaves them without guilt while improving their domestic affairs.

Keil and Delitzsch describe the folds as stone enclosures, citing Wetstein on the nomads of the Leja, and take the building of towns as rebuilding and fortification; Ellicott agrees on both, the verb often meaning to build up or repair.
Clarke argues from impossibility, following Calmet: they could only have meant repairing the Amorite cities lately taken.

Clarke asks who could hold the fenced cities and answers with the census — 110,580 men in the two tribes and a half, of whom only 40,000 crossed, leaving 70,580 behind; Wesley reaches the same conclusion from the words themselves.

Ellicott renders the pledge as equipping themselves in haste and takes "little ones" of the whole defenceless part of the nation; Keil and Delitzsch fix the term of service by an event, the bringing of Israel to its place.
Gill reads the emphasis as a direct answer to the charge of cowardice.

18.pericope_label: the pledge not to return, and the surrender of any claim west of Jordan

schools.summary: Gill takes the pledge at full weight — houses, families, flocks and herds left behind until every man in Israel has his inheritance — and denies that the renunciation was defiance or contempt of the good land.

Ellicott treats the verse as a crux for the term rendered "on yonder side" and "on this side", concluding that nothing can be inferred from it about where the writer stood; Keil and Delitzsch carry the speech through as one continuous undertaking.
Henry counts the renunciation as the fourth article of a fair and generous proposal, leaving so much the more on the far side for their brethren.

themes: not returning until all are settled

schools.summary: Ellicott shows that only the object of the phrase has changed, infers that Israel's army was regarded as the LORD's, and gathers the places where the ark went into war.

Gill records that Moses was now better satisfied; Calvin raises the objection that Moses extended boundaries God had fixed and answered without consulting him, and resolves it from the outcome and from the later approbation of the ruling.
Henry marks the substitution: they offered to go before the children of Israel, Moses requires them to go before the LORD, since the cause is God's more than their brethren's.
Wesley identifies "before the LORD" as before the ark, the token of God's presence.
Gill sets out how thoroughly Moses tries them — over Jordan, all of them, and before the LORD — and notes how exactly the crossing was afterwards performed in those terms.
Henry states the practical form of the condition: they were never to lay down their arms till their brethren laid down theirs.
Keil and Delitzsch treat the following verses as one conditional grant with its penalty clause attached.

themes: until he hath driven out his enemies
a term God alone can close

fidelity.note: the observation that the tribes' own wording left the term of service conveniently open, and that Moses replaces it, is the summary's inference from the two verses rather than a comment any witness makes

schools.summary: Gill explains the subduing before the LORD as done in his presence, by his power, and for his people.
Henry draws out the double clearance — guiltless before God and blameless before Israel — and applies it to any possession we come to.
Wesley glosses the phrase as denoting God's presence and his gracious and powerful assistance.
Ellicott points forward to where the eastern grant is recorded as accomplished.

fidelity.note: the closing paragraph, that the verse never treats the eastern country as second-best, is read off the verse itself rather than taken from a witness, though it agrees with Henry on the possession being held guiltless

23.pericope_label: the warning against breaking the pledge, and the charge to build

schools.summary: Gill keeps the failure in view as a failure of the promise given; Calvin treats the words as a formal protestation summoning them before the tribunal of God, and explains why "your sin will find you out" is stronger than saying they will not escape.
Henry marks the direction of the offence — against the LORD, and not against their brethren only — and warns that God will reckon with them though they make light of it.
Wesley reads "your sin" as its punishment and turns the sentence into counsel: find your sins out, that you may repent of them and forsake them.

themes: be sure your sin will find you out
their own words made a command

25.pericope_label: the two tribes bind themselves to the terms

schools.summary: Gill divides the answer between the two halves of the bargain — the march before the LORD and the provision for children and flocks — and reports Jarchi on the singular verb.
Keil and Delitzsch note that the promise is repeated and that its verb stands in the singular, as through a spokesman.
Henry treats the speech as a bond given for performance, and supplies the equity behind it: their brethren had helped conquer this country, so justice bound them to the conquest of their brethren's.
Henry sees Moses settling the matter with Eleazar and with Joshua his successor, knowing he will not live to see it perfected, and leaving an estate upon condition for Joshua to declare absolute.

Gill is careful not to overstate Moses' personal authority, allowing that the court may have consented; Calvin insists the elders were united with him in the decision, and explains the conditions as protecting both an honest performance and against a deceitful one.

themes: a record that protects both ways

29.pericope_label: the conditional grant entrusted to Eleazar and Joshua

schools.summary: Gill identifies the hearers as Eleazar, Joshua and the princes and glosses the failure as a change of mind and a broken promise; Calvin reads the two branches as one principle, the alternative being compulsion rather than a consolation portion, and notes that legislating for a division not yet possible encourages confidence.
Henry hears the distinction in the form of the sentence: not no inheritance at all, but not this inheritance which they covet.
Wesley states the penalty plainly — they forfeit Gilead and are constrained to seek possessions among their brethren.
Keil and Delitzsch keep the two conditional clauses in their formal shape.

themes: confidence in a victory not yet won

31.pericope_label: the two tribes answer as one man

schools.summary: Gill draws attention to the singular verb as a mark of unanimity, reporting Jarchi, and notes how often the undertaking has now been repeated for confirmation.
Wesley opens out the appeal, taking "as the LORD hath said" either of the present word through Moses or of the old command to go in and possess.

Keil and Delitzsch render the second clause as a request that the inheritance remain to them beyond Jordan; Ellicott notes that the ambiguous term for the river's sides stands here without its qualifying words.
Henry marks the repetition simply as their adhering to their brethren.

Ellicott and Keil and Delitzsch both find the late appearance of half Manasseh strange and explain it from the conquests recorded next; Keil and Delitzsch give the extent of the grant in the terms the Hebrew uses.

Gill wonders whether the grant was by word of mouth or by a signed instrument; Calvin insists Moses laid down an inviolable law on God's command, and hears an implied contrast with the covenant made with Abraham.
Henry suggests the land proved too much for two tribes, and that a warlike family was the right one to plant on a frontier.

debates.question: Why does the half tribe of Manasseh appear only at the close of the grant?

sides.position: because that part of the tribe had conquered the districts and so acquired a just claim to them
because the land proved too much for two tribes, so a half tribe was given a lot among them

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch identify each town on the ground, from Dibon north of the Arnon to Jogbehah near Amman, and correct v. Raumer on which Aroer is meant; Ellicott renders "built" as repaired or fortified, traces the later redistribution of the towns, and notes that the Moabite stone was found at Dibon.
Gill takes the building as repair of walls and houses demolished in the wars with Sihon and Og, and supplies the later names of Bethharan.

Wesley explains that the old cities were not burnt as several in Canaan were, so repair was all that was needed; Clarke follows Aroer through Emim, Moabite, Amorite and Israelite hands to the Assyrian captivity and back to Moab.

sides.position: the Aroer in the middle of the valley of the Arnon
the Aroer before Rabbah, allotted to Gad
holders: v. Raumer (as reported by Keil and Delitzsch)

37.pericope_label: the cities the Reubenites rebuilt, and the changing of their names

schools.summary: Gill argues from Heshbon and Elealeh that the towns were repaired rather than founded, collects the traditions about Kirjathaim, and notes that the Moabites afterwards restored the old names.
Keil and Delitzsch fix Heshbon and Elealeh on the ground and follow the title of Heshbon from Reuben to Gad and on to the Levites.
Henry gives both motives for the renaming and puts his weight on the burying of idolatrous names in oblivion.
Wesley allows either the custom of conquerors or the prohibition against naming other gods; Clarke takes the renaming simply as what conquerors did.

debates.question: Why were the names of Nebo and Baal-meon changed?

sides.position: to purge idolatrous names the people were forbidden to mention
because conquerors customarily renamed the cities they took

39.pericope_label: Machir takes Gilead, and Moses confirms it to his house

schools.summary: Ellicott renders the opening as a pluperfect and treats the verse as the belated explanation of half Manasseh's inclusion; Keil and Delitzsch justify the pluperfect from Hebrew narrative style and map the Manassite share.

Calvin weighs and rejects the view that the conquest followed the grant, without pressing the point; Gill distinguishes the Gilead already conquered from the part still in Amorite hands, and denies that Machir himself received it.
Wesley says plainly that the grant was to the posterity of Machir, not the man.

debates.question: Did the Machirites take Gilead before or after Moses made the eastern grant?

sides.position: before — the verbs are pluperfect, and the conquest is the reason the grant excepts their portion
after, attracted by the advantage that presented itself — a view Calvin declines to contend against

debates.question: Was Gilead given to Machir himself?

sides.position: to his family and posterity, Machir being long dead
to Machir in person, he being still alive

schools.summary: Ellicott and Keil and Delitzsch trace Jair through Segub and Hezron to a daughter of Machir, making him a great-grandson of Manasseh reckoned to his maternal tribe; Keil and Delitzsch suggest a rich dowry as the reason, and give the extent of the conquest in Argob.
Gill states the anomaly at once, that Jair was of Manasseh by his mother and of Judah otherwise.
Clarke would have translated Havoth-jair as the villages of Jair, and quotes Ainsworth on these tribes being first settled and first carried captive.

outliers.note: sets the honour of being first to receive an inheritance against the judgement of being first carried into Assyrian captivity.

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch place Nobah among the Machirites, identify Kenath with Kanatha of Coelesyria and the Decapolis, describe its extensive ruins, and decline Kurtz's identification of the site.
Gill admits that who Nobah was is not certain, and passes on the tradition that he was born in Egypt and buried beyond Jordan.

Wesley infers an eminent man of Manasseh, and closes on the reversal — placed before the other tribes, and displaced before them; Clarke had already given the custom of conquerors naming cities after themselves.

outliers.note: reject the identification of Nobah with the village of Nowa in Jolan, holding that the name has not been preserved at all.

themes: a name that did not hold
